source.title: Causal Concept Graphs in LLM Latent Space for Stepwise Reasoning
source.authors: Md Muntaqim Meherab; Noori Mohammad; Faiza Feroz

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses task-conditioned sparse autoencoders to create concept features for its causal-graph method. Its experiments evaluate graph-guided intervention scores, not whether superposition occurs or whether SAE features recover canonical model features.
record.gate_note: The paper cites superposition as motivation and reports SAE activation sparsity and a qualitative correlation comparison; these do not test the claim that sparse feature overlap emerges under capacity pressure or establish SAE recovery of underlying features. CFS comparisons, graph-density results, and sparsity-sweep CFS results concern the proposed graph method's performance, not the claim versions. The ROME-style comparison is a lightweight adapted baseline, not an original-method test.
record.test_reason: The paper uses task-conditioned TopK SAEs on GPT-2 Medium as a tool for concept discovery, then learns DAGs over the SAE features. It reports only its own method's performance: CFS, graph density, ablations and SAE training diagnostics. It never measures whether features are superposed, whether polysemanticity stems from capacity pressure, or whether SAE features are canonical, stable or complete units. Superposition is cited only as motivation (ref. 6).
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors conclude that CCG outperforms their adapted ROME-style, SAE-only and random baselines on CFS (5.654 vs 3.382, 2.479 and 1.032). They say the gap to SAE-only suggests the learned graph separates causally upstream concepts from merely active ones. They describe the graphs as partial diagnostic evidence and draw no conclusions about superposition.
record.recipe_differences: This is not a reproduction of Toy Models of Superposition. It uses task-conditioned TopK SAEs and DAG learning to study concept interactions in GPT-2 Medium, rather than testing toy-network superposition geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that TopK sparsity changes CFS, extraction layer changes cosine-distance separability, edge sparsity affects graph size and CFS, and removing the DAG constraint lowers CFS. These sensitivities concern CCG performance, not the claim versions.

fits_no_version.finding: In the TopK sweep, the authors assert that larger k (25, 50) 'reintroduces polysemanticity'. They give no polysemanticity measure; the only reported outcome is CFS, which peaks at k=13.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE sparsity level trades off downstream causal-graph usefulness; the claim that higher k increases polysemanticity is asserted, not measured.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 1's L0 rates (41.4%, 30.1%, 29.3%) conflict with the stated deterministic TopK=13, which implies 5.1%, and with the prose saying 5.1% was reached by epoch 30.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reporting of SAE activation rate in this study is internally inconsistent.

fits_no_version.finding: Beta decorrelation regularisation qualitatively reduces off-diagonal correlations among SAE concepts. The evidence is figure-only and confounded by a NaN bug.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Covariance penalties may modestly decorrelate SAE concept activations.

record.problems: Only GPT-2 Medium is studied. The SAE uses imposed TopK sparsity, so the reported sparse codes do not establish recovery of underlying model features. The paper gives inconsistent L0-rate reporting between Table 1 and the prose. The β-regularisation correlation comparison has a stated computation bug and is qualitative. The paper also notes that its ROME-style baseline is a lightweight adaptation rather than the original tracing procedure.
record.rows_left_out: No rows for the CFS tables, graph density, or CFS ablations: these report performance of the proposed graph method, not outcomes about the claim versions. No result was dropped from the claim-relevant SAE activation-rate or correlation findings recorded above.

untested.parts: All of it. There are no toy models, no feature-count versus dimension manipulation, no sparsity phase transition and no geometry analysis.
All of it. Capacity competition and importance-based allocation are never measured.
All of it. Non-capacity causes of polysemanticity are not examined.

Whether GPT-2 Medium features are distributed across neurons, or whether the SAE recovers genuine sparse model features. The SAE's sparsity is imposed, and the only quality check is a 100% reasoning-type probe that the authors say may reflect prompt-format cues.
Completeness, stability across seeds or SAE sizes, and canonicality of SAE features. The reported seed stability concerns graph CFS, not features.
All of it. One-dimensional and multi-dimensional features are never compared.

record.verdict_notes: Only GPT-2 Medium, layer 12, 300 examples per dataset. The SAE uses imposed TopK sparsity plus a decorrelation penalty, so nothing here bears on natural superposition or on SAE feature canonicality. The CFS baselines are lightweight adaptations. No instructions were found in the text.

versions.untested_parts: No test of more features than dimensions, overlapping near-orthogonal feature directions, a sparsity-dependent superposition transition, or regular superposition geometry.
No test of polysemanticity arising from competition for limited representational capacity or of importance determining dedicated versus shared dimensions.
No test of alternative causes of polysemanticity or whether polysemanticity alone indicates superposition.
The paper trains an SAE with imposed TopK sparsity, but does not test whether its features recover naturally occurring model features or whether model features are distributed across neurons.
No test that SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of the model's representation.
No comparison of one-dimensional features with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: GPT-2 Medium
rows.operation_detail: Measured task-conditioned SAE L0 activation rate during training.
rows.note: TopK=13, K=256 was used. The reported rate is for the SAE codes, not evidence that the SAE recovered underlying model features.
rows.check: This is a training diagnostic of the study's own SAE, not a claim-relevant measurement, and arguably should not be a row. Sparsity is imposed by TopK (k=13 of 256), so the L0 rate says nothing about natural sparsity in the model.

rows.subject: GPT-2 Medium
rows.operation_detail: Compared concept correlations in SAEs trained without and with β-regularisation.
rows.baseline: SAE without β; numeric value not stated
rows.value: With β=0.1, off-diagonal correlations appear slightly reduced
rows.note: Authors describe this only as qualitative evidence. They report NaNs from zero-variance TopK columns and defer a corrected ablation.
rows.check: A qualitative, figure-only comparison of SAE concept correlations under the study's own decorrelation regulariser. The authors flag it as confounded by a NaN computation bug. It measures the effect of an SAE design choice, not superposition.
